text: Johnson draws from this a further praise, and gives it his accustomed plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He thought that other dramatists had lifted their persons above the common level of humanity, and had furnished them with sentiments which no living man would express, and with a diction contrived rather to raise admiration than to produce belief. Shakespeare’s refusal of this elevation Johnson therefore reckons among his chief merits. His persons speak as the reader would have spoken in the same situation and under the same pressure; their words are taken from ordinary life, and they affect us because we recognise ourselves in them. The same naturalness remains where the incidents themselves are removed from probability. A ghost upon the platform, or witches upon the heath, belong to a region outside common experience; but the speech of those who behold them is still within the bounds of such experience. In Shakespeare the marvellous is in the action, while the dialogue keeps the level of life; Hamlet questions his father’s spirit as any son might question an apparition so dreadful, and Macbeth broods over the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood over the promise of a crown.
